explanation.body:
At constant pressure, $\frac{V_1}{V_2}=\frac{T_1}{T_2}$. For a fixed mass, $\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}=\frac{V_1}{V_2}$.

Thus $\frac{\rho_2}{1.20}=\frac{20+273.15}{27+273.15}$, giving $\rho_2=1.172\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.

perOption.A: Uses the Celsius ratio $20/27$ in place of the kelvin ratio.

difficultyReason: Relates the volume and density ratios and converts both temperatures to kelvin.
misconception: Using Celsius temperatures in gas-law ratios
transcription:
The density of air is $1.20\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ at a temperature of $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and atmospheric pressure.

Assuming that the air behaves as an ideal gas, what is the density of air at a temperature of $27\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and atmospheric pressure?

A $0.89\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$
B $1.17\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$
C $1.23\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$
D $1.62\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$

explanation.body: The heat lost by X equals the heat gained by Y, so $mc(80-T)=2m(2c)(T-30)$. This gives $80-T=4T-120$, hence $T=40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

perOption.A: Leaves Y at its initial temperature despite heat transfer from X.
perOption.C: Takes the arithmetic mean as if the blocks had equal heat capacities.
perOption.D: Reverses the heat-capacity weighting of X and Y.

difficultyReason: Requires weighting the two temperature changes by the blocks’ different heat capacities.
misconception: Averaging temperatures without weighting by heat capacity
transcription:
A metal block X of mass $m$, specific heat capacity $c$ and temperature $80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is placed in good thermal contact with a second metal block Y of mass $2m$, specific heat capacity $2c$ and temperature $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Assuming there is no energy loss to the surroundings, what will be the final temperature of both blocks?

A $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$
B $40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$
C $55\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$
D $70\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$

explanation.body: The kinetic-energy graph repeats every $200\ \mathrm{ms}$, so the motion has period $T=400\ \mathrm{ms}$. Using $E_{\mathrm{K,max}}=\tfrac12m\omega^2x_0^2=1.0\ \mathrm{J}$ gives $x_0=0.30\ \mathrm{m}$. Hence $a_{\max}=\omega^2x_0=74\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: Uses 90.0 as the mass in kilograms and 400 as the period in seconds.
perOption.B: Combines the gram and millisecond conversion errors with the shorter energy period.
perOption.C: Uses half the correct angular frequency, as if the motion took 800 ms per cycle.

difficultyReason: Requires inferring the motion period from the energy graph and using peak energy to find acceleration.
misconception: Confusing the kinetic-energy period with the SHM period
transcription:
A particle of a mass of $90.0\ \mathrm{g}$ undergoes simple harmonic motion. The graph shows the variation of its kinetic energy, $E_{\mathrm{K}}$ with time, $t$.

[Graph of $E_{\mathrm{K}}$ in J against $t$ in ms. The smooth periodic curve is zero at 0, 200 and 400 ms and peaks at 1.0 J at 100 and 300 ms.]

What is the maximum acceleration of the particle?

A $0.074\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
B $0.148\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
C $37\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
D $74\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$

explanation.body: The shadow moves in simple harmonic motion, so its speed is zero at the turning points. Its maximum speed is $\omega x_0=\frac{2\pi}{2.16}\times0.500=1.45\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Treats the maximum speed as constant throughout the motion.
perOption.B: Assumes constant speed and uses the value of the maximum acceleration as a speed.
perOption.D: Uses the numerical value of the maximum acceleration as the maximum speed.

issues: The key assumes an orthographic projection with parallel light rays. A finite-distance point lamp generally gives a different shadow motion and maximum speed.
difficultyReason: Requires recognising that a projection of uniform circular motion has a varying speed.
misconception: Assuming the shadow inherits the bob’s constant speed
transcription:
A conical pendulum undergoes uniform circular motion in a horizontal plane. The radius of the circular path is $0.500\ \mathrm{m}$ and the time taken to complete one revolution is $2.16\ \mathrm{s}$. A lamp shines on the pendulum bob as shown.

[The bob hangs on an inclined string and moves around a dashed horizontal circular path. The lamp is to the left and the vertical screen is to the right.]

The shadow of the bob on the screen was observed to move back and forth along a horizontal line with

A constant speed of $1.45\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
B constant speed of $4.23\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
C speed varying between 0 and $1.45\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
D speed varying between 0 and $4.23\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

explanation.body: A stable interference pattern requires a constant phase difference between the sources. Similar amplitudes give a clear pattern because very unequal amplitudes give little contrast between maxima and minima. The waves must overlap, and perpendicular polarisations prevent interference.

perOption.A: A constant phase difference can be nonzero.
perOption.B: Correct. Similar amplitudes give clear contrast.
perOption.C: The school’s explanation requires the paths to intersect so the waves overlap.
perOption.D: The school notes that the waves can be unpolarised, provided they have components that can interfere.

difficultyReason: Requires distinguishing the conditions for fringe contrast from the condition for stability.
misconception: Equating coherence with zero phase difference

explanation.body: After $4\ \mathrm{s}$, shift the left pulse $4\ \mathrm{cm}$ right and the right pulse $4\ \mathrm{cm}$ left, as in the key’s overlay. Add their signed displacements at each position. The two rising slopes add in the overlap, with a downward jump at each end.

perOption.B: Smooths away the jumps made by the vertical pulse edges.
perOption.C: Loses the outer slopes by treating too much of the pulses as overlapping.
perOption.D: Cancels the rising segments across the overlap even though their sum varies with position.

difficultyReason: Requires translating both asymmetric pulses and adding signed displacements over the overlap.
misconception: Adding pulse magnitudes instead of signed displacements
transcription:
Two waves approach each other with speed $1\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$, as shown in the figure below.

[On a grid with 1 cm horizontal squares, count columns from 0 at the left border and measure displacements in vertical squares from the baseline. The rightward pulse drops vertically to −1 at column 2, rises to +1 at column 4, then returns to zero at column 5. The leftward pulse falls from zero at column 8 to −1 at column 9, rises to +1 at column 11, then drops vertically to zero.]

Which of the following gives the result of the superposition of the waves $4\ \mathrm{s}$ later?

[A: Zero to column 4, down to −1 at 5, up to zero at 6, then a vertical drop to −1. It rises to +1 at 7, drops vertically to zero there, rises to +1 at 8 and falls to zero at 9.]
[B: Zero to column 4, down to −1 at 5, flat to 6, up to +1 at 8, flat to 9, then down to zero at 10.]
[C: Zero to column 5, then a vertical drop to −1, flat to 6, up to +1 at 7, flat to 8, then a vertical drop to zero.]
[D: Zero to column 4, down to −1 at 5, flat to 6, then a vertical rise to zero. Zero to column 8, then a vertical rise to +1, flat to 9 and down to zero at 10.]

explanation.body: Add the signed point-charge potentials at O, using the distances from O to the charges. This gives $V=V_1+V_2=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{-7.4\times10^{-9}}{0.49}+\frac{3.6\times10^{-9}}{0.36}\right)=-46\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Swaps the distances to the positive and negative charges.
perOption.B: Uses 45 cm in place of the 49 cm distance to the negative charge.
perOption.D: Drops the negative sign of the contribution from the negative charge.

issues: The key labels the target Q instead of O and repeats $Q_1/r_1$ in its factored expression. Its unfactored expression and numerical answer use the correct contributions.
difficultyReason: Requires selecting the two distances to the target point and adding signed scalar contributions.
misconception: Using the separation between charges in the potential calculation
transcription:
Two fixed point charges of magnitudes $Q_1=-7.4\ \mathrm{nC}$ and $Q_2=+3.6\ \mathrm{nC}$, are located at points X and Y respectively. Their distances from another point O and from each other are shown below.

[X and Y lie on a horizontal line, with X to the left of Y and $XY=45\ \mathrm{cm}$. Point O lies below the line, with $XO=49\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $YO=36\ \mathrm{cm}$.]

What is the value of the potential at point O?

A $-120\ \mathrm{V}$
B $-56\ \mathrm{V}$
C $-46\ \mathrm{V}$
D $220\ \mathrm{V}$

explanation.body: The electric field points from higher to lower potential and is given by $E=-\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}r}$. A uniform potential around a point has zero gradient there, so the electric field is zero.

perOption.A: A zero field fixes the gradient at zero and leaves the value of the potential undetermined.
perOption.B: A uniform nonzero field gives a constant nonzero potential gradient.
perOption.D: Differentiates the electric field in place of taking the negative gradient of potential.

difficultyReason: Requires distinguishing the value of a potential from its spatial gradient.
misconception: Confusing zero potential with zero potential gradient

explanation.body: Electrons and protons have opposite charges and travel in opposite directions, so their conventional currents add. Using a charge magnitude of $1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$ for each particle, $I=I_e+I_p=(5.0\times10^{18})(1.6\times10^{-19})+(2.0\times10^{18})(1.6\times10^{-19})=1.1\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: Counts an effective rate of only $1.0 \times 10^{18}$ elementary charges per second.
perOption.B: Subtracts the two current contributions because the particles move in opposite directions.

difficultyReason: Requires recognising that opposite charges moving in opposite directions produce currents in the same direction.
transcription:
A high electric potential difference is applied between two electrodes of a hydrogen discharge tube so that the gas is ionized. Electrons then move towards the positive electrode and protons towards the negative electrode. In each second, $5.0\times10^{18}$ electrons and $2.0\times10^{18}$ protons pass a cross-section of the tube. What is the current, in amperes, flowing in the discharge tube?

A 0.16
B 0.48
C 0.80
D 1.1

explanation.body: Moving the slider in A, B or D changes the voltage across the lamp. In C, the lamp is connected directly across the supply terminals, so its voltage stays fixed.

perOption.A: The slider varies the voltage between the tap and the negative terminal.
perOption.B: The slider varies the resistance in series with the lamp and thus its voltage.
perOption.D: The slider varies the voltage between the positive terminal and the tap.

issues: The batch labels this item as text, but the four circuit diagrams are essential and the extracted text does not represent their connections.
difficultyReason: Requires tracing the lamp terminals in four variable-resistor configurations.
misconception: Assuming a parallel resistor can vary the load voltage of an ideal supply

explanation.body: The T–S–R branch is in parallel with the upper branch, so it does not enter the divider calculation. The two resistors from U to R take a share of the $10.0\ \mathrm{V}$ across T–U–Q–R, giving $V_{UR}=\frac{50+50}{50+50+50}\times10.0=6.67\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Uses the full supply voltage across T–R for the smaller section U–R.
perOption.B: Assigns too much of the supply voltage to U–R by undercounting the drop across T–U.
perOption.D: Assigns too little of the supply voltage to the two resistors between U and R.

issues: The key writes QR in the divider formula, but its numerator and answer are for U–Q–R.
difficultyReason: Requires identifying the two relevant resistors within one branch of a parallel network.
misconception: Including a parallel branch in a series potential-divider ratio
transcription:
Five resistors, each of resistance $50\ \Omega$, are connected in a loop as shown below. A $10.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery of negligible internal resistance is connected across TR.

[The loop follows T–U–Q–R–S–T, with one resistor on each segment. The battery connects T to R, with its positive terminal at T.]

What is the potential difference between points U and R?

A $10.0\ \mathrm{V}$
B $8.7\ \mathrm{V}$
C $6.7\ \mathrm{V}$
D $3.7\ \mathrm{V}$

explanation.body: The right-hand grip rule gives an anticlockwise magnetic field around X, with a downward component at P and an upward component at Q. Applying Fleming’s left-hand rule to the rightward current in Y gives a force into the page at P and out of the page at Q.

perOption.A: Reverses the force directions at both points.
perOption.C: Treats the force as radial to X, although it must be perpendicular to the current in Y.
perOption.D: Applies the attraction rule for parallel currents to perpendicular wires.

difficultyReason: Requires combining the right-hand grip rule with Fleming’s left-hand rule at two points.
misconception: Applying parallel-wire attraction rules to perpendicular wires
transcription:
Two long straight wires X and Y are placed perpendicular to each other at a distance $d$ apart. A current flows out of the page in wire X. The same current flows from left to right in wire Y.

What are the directions of the forces acting on wire Y at the point P and Q due to the magnetic field produced by wire X?

[Wire Y lies horizontally with current $I$ to the right. Wire X is shown end-on with a dot, a perpendicular distance $d$ above Y. P and Q lie on Y to the left and right of X respectively.]

Option | force at P | force at Q
A | out of page | into page
B | into page | out of page
C | towards X | away from X
D | towards X | towards X

explanation.body: The induced e.m.f. equals the rate of increase of flux linkage while the coil enters the field. The area inside the field increases at rate $Hv$, so $E=BHv$.

perOption.A: Correct. Increasing $L$ extends the entry time.
perOption.B: Increasing $H$ increases the area entering the field per second.
perOption.C: Increasing $v$ increases the area entering the field per second.
perOption.D: Increasing $B$ increases the flux through each unit of area.

issues: The question diagram depicts the field into the page and the key diagram depicts it out of the page. The magnitude of the induced e.m.f. is the same.
difficultyReason: Requires identifying which coil dimension controls how fast the area inside the field changes.
misconception: Confusing total flux change with its rate of change

explanation.body:
The mean power is $\langle P\rangle=\tfrac12P_0=3.0\ \mathrm{W}$. From $P_0=I_0^2R$, the peak current is $I_0=2.0\ \mathrm{A}$.

Using $\langle P\rangle=V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/R$ gives $V_{\mathrm{rms}}\approx2.1\ \mathrm{V}$. The power period is half the current period, so the source frequency is $1/0.040=25\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

perOption.A: Mistakes mean power for peak power divided by the sinusoidal current’s factor of $\sqrt{2}$.
perOption.C: Misuses the mean-power relation: $4.5\ \mathrm{V^2}$ is the square of the r.m.s. voltage.
perOption.D: Uses the power waveform’s frequency as the source frequency.

issues: The key gives an r.m.s. voltage of 3.0 V, which is the peak voltage. Its mean-power equation gives 2.1 V r.m.s.
difficultyReason: Requires reading peak power and separating the power period from the current period.
misconception: Taking the power period as the source period
transcription:
The figure below shows the power supplied by a sinusoidal a.c. source to a load of resistance $1.5\ \Omega$ over $60\ \mathrm{ms}$.

[Graph of power in W against time in ms. The curve is zero at 0, 20, 40 and 60 ms and peaks at 6 W at 10, 30 and 50 ms.]

Which of the following is correct?

A The mean value of the power supplied is $4.2\ \mathrm{W}$.
B The peak value of the current supplied is $2.0\ \mathrm{A}$.
C The root mean square value of the voltage supplied is $4.5\ \mathrm{V}$.
D The frequency of the source is $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

explanation.body: The key’s current paths show C shunting the half-cycle that would drive current upward through the load. D shunts the opposite half-cycle, leaving load current flowing upward, which gives the reverse of the marked polarity.

perOption.A: The series diode in the upper wire allows downward current through the load on the conducting half-cycle.
perOption.B: The series diode in the lower wire also allows downward current through the load on the conducting half-cycle.
perOption.C: The shunt diode conducts on the half-cycle that would make the lower load terminal positive.
perOption.D: Correct. The load polarity is reversed.

issues: The shunt circuits C and D require source or series impedance to limit current on the clamped half-cycle. With an ideal zero-impedance voltage source they would short it during that half-cycle. The extracted text also omits the circuit connections and diode directions.
difficultyReason: Requires tracking which half-cycle a series or shunt diode passes to the load.
misconception: Ignoring the polarity of the half-cycle passed by the diode
